query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Under sustained loading at intermediate temperatures, progressive plastic deformation in nanoscale fcc/bcc high-entropy-alloy multilayers is governed primarily by a coupled mechanism of partial-dislocation nucleation and glide, moderated by local short-range ordering at the interfaces, which promotes intermittent dislocation activity and stable accumulations of plastic strain over time.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoscale fcc/bcc HEA multilayers with uniform layer thicknesses and intentionally prepared short-range ordering (SRO), minimal preexisting defects, and controlled chemical compositions to ensure a stable interface microstructure.
generation.intervention: Vary the applied stress (sub-yield and near-yield) and temperature (room temperature to moderate ranges) in an in-situ nanoindentation creep experiment, coupled with crystal-plasticity simulations to track partial-dislocation activity and local SRO variations at the layer interfaces.
generation.conditions: The coatings remain nanoscale in thickness, with composition tuned to preserve fcc/bcc layering and intentionally moderate SRO; mechanical tests involve sustained loads for extended durations at discrete temperature increments.
generation.structural_mediator: Short-range ordering (SRO) at or near the fcc/bcc interface and within the high-entropy-alloy layers, which modifies dislocation structure and mobility.
generation.mechanism: Partial dislocations repeatedly nucleate at or near the interfaces. These dislocations are slowed by local chemical disorder and the associated lattice distortions, producing a stable, but progressive, accumulation of plastic strain. As loading continues, SRO regions on the fcc/bcc interfaces concentrate lattice strain energy that hinders long-range dislocation glide and leads to time-dependent creep behavior dominated by intermittent partial-dislocation motion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to baseline multilayers with reduced SRO or simpler compositions, the SRO-containing multilayers will exhibit lower but persistent creep rates, with electron microscopy revealing stable pinned partial dislocations in regions of higher local SRO and a more pronounced time-dependent accumulation of lattice defects under constant load.
generation.baseline: Multilayers of similar geometry and thickness but with negligible short-range order or simpler alloy compositions. These baseline coatings would display more conventional dislocation glide and a faster transition to steady-state creep, lacking pronounced pinned partials within the interfaces.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate only if the SRO is sufficiently developed to impede dislocation glide and the layer thickness is in the 10–100 nm range where interface effects strongly influence dislocation behavior at moderate testing temperatures. Extreme temperatures or stress levels well beyond the yield point may shift the controlling mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: The relative importance of partial dislocation activity versus alternative pathways (e.g., grain-boundary or interface diffusional creep) under different compositions and temperature-stress regimes remains to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of fcc/bcc HEA multilayers: one with negligible SRO (e.g., simpler composition or quenched processing) and one engineered to promote SRO (e.g., by adjusting compositional complexity and using appropriate thermal treatments). Perform in-situ nanoindentation creep tests at several loads and moderate temperatures while conducting in-situ TEM or X-ray diffraction to monitor dislocation evolution.
measurements: Indentation creep curves and steady-state creep rates for each set of samples under equivalent normalized loads and temperatures.
TEM characterization or high-resolution diffraction to quantify partial-dislocation structure, stacking-fault densities, and interface morphology evolution.
Comparisons of dislocation densities and pinned partial dislocations in SRO- versus non-SRO samples.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If SRO-enhanced samples do not exhibit significantly decreased but sustained creep rates or if partial dislocation activity at the interfaces is absent, then the proposed mechanism that SRO-mediated partial-dislocation dynamics dominate progressive deformation would be invalidated.

cited_evidence.text: Owing to the outstanding softening resistance and thermal stability of BCC-structured refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs), their unique deformation-induced defect structures merit investigation. Therefore, this study evaluated the mechanical properties and deformation behaviors of W-based low- to high-entropy alloys at various temperatures and orientations using nanoindentation and microcompression, complemented by post-mortem TEM and atomistic simulations to observe dislocation populations and their evolution. Results reveal that HEAs exhibit reduced elastic and plastic anisotropy while retaining high-temperature strength. With increasing compositional complexity, planar slip and abrupt stress drops were progressively replaced by homogeneous flow and smoother serrations. Severe lattice distortion promoted dislocation nucleation but impeded long-range glide, enabling cooperative edge and screw dislocation activity that sustained strength and work hardening across temperatures.

Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study AlxCrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5.
